draw.text: How the nuclear model of the atom was discovered

explain.say: Look at the start. In 1803, John Dalton said everything is made of tiny solid balls called atoms. Then in 1897, J. J. Thomson found electrons, tiny negative particles inside atoms. So in 1904 he suggested the plum pudding model. Can you guess what it looked like?

explain.say: Yes, a ball of positive charge with electrons dotted through it, like fruit in a pudding! Now 1909. Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at very thin gold foil. Most went straight through, but a few bounced back! Was the atom solid, then?

explain.say: Mostly empty space! In 1911 Rutherford explained it: nearly all the mass is in a tiny, dense, positive centre called the nucleus. That is the nuclear model. In 1913 Niels Bohr put the electrons in fixed shells. What is in the middle of the atom?

explain.say: The nucleus, perfect! Finally, in 1932, James Chadwick found the neutron. Each new experiment improved the model; that is how science works. Wow fact: if an atom were a football stadium, its nucleus would be about the size of a pea. Challenge: draw all four models in a row!

faq.q: What was the plum pudding model?
faq.a: J. J. Thomson's 1904 model: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons spread through it, like fruit in a pudding.

faq.q: What did the gold foil experiment show?
faq.a: Most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space. A few bounced back, so there must be a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.

faq.q: What is the nuclear model of the atom?
faq.a: A tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus holding nearly all the mass, surrounded by electrons in mostly empty space.
In 1913 Bohr suggested that electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed distances, or energy levels, called shells.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. It has no charge and sits in the nucleus with the protons.

facts: The gold foil experiment (1909) was carried out by Geiger and Marsden under Rutherford.
An atom's nucleus is about 100 000 times smaller across than the atom itself.

quiz.say: Why did most alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil?
quiz.show: Why did most alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil?
quiz.why: Most of the atom is empty space, so most particles met nothing to deflect them.

wrong.0: Softness was not the reason; the foil's atoms are mostly empty.
wrong.1: Being invisible does not let them pass through matter.

quiz.say: Which model came straight before the nuclear model?
quiz.show: Which model came straight before the nuclear model?
quiz.why: Thomson's 1904 plum pudding model was replaced by Rutherford's nuclear model in 1911.

wrong.1: Bohr's model came after Rutherford's, in 1913.
wrong.2: The neutron was discovered in 1932, much later.
